- Move release authority into the Callisto CLI: immutable intent, provider observation, fresh-runner recovery, terminal receipts, and explicit source/orchestration provenance.
- Build, attest, manifest, and upload product artifacts for macOS ARM, Linux GNU, Linux musl, and WASI.
- Make GitHub Actions a thin adapter with isolated checkouts, secret-free plan/build jobs, and credentials confined to execution.
- Require release evidence before merge without an Environment approval gate.
- Use the hermetic provider harness as the current rehearsal boundary; no AWS or staging registry.

## Verification
- `just ci` — passed: 1,399 tests, clippy, docs, audit, WASI, and 90.54% line coverage.
- `just release-workflow-behavior` — passed: 11 durable lifecycle scenarios.
- Artifact build-script and workflow-contract checks pass locally.

## Deliberate follow-up
- Hosted CI must execute the four production build recipes.

1	# Self-release lifecycle
2	
3	This document is the operational contract for Callisto's own releases. The implementation plan
4	is [`SPEC-SELF-RELEASE-LIFECYCLE`](projects/SPEC-SELF-RELEASE-LIFECYCLE.json).
5	
6	## Authority
7	
8	A verified merge of a managed Callisto release PR is the sole authorization for publication.
9	There is no GitHub Environment reviewer, deployment protection gate, or second manual click.
10	Merge evidence and release authorization are separate concerns: required CI checks protect the
11	merge; the merge authorizes the release.
12	
13	## Merge evidence
14	
15	The active `main` ruleset requires one approving review, signed commits, linear squash history,
16	and the following named evidence before a release PR can merge:
17	
18	- `Workflow Contracts`
19	- `Code Formatting (Moon & Just)`
20	- `Clippy Lints (Moon & Just)`
21	- `Security & Advisory Audit (Moon & Just)`
22	- `Code Coverage & Test Report`
23	- `Test Suite & WASM Check (macos-latest)`
24	- `Test Suite & WASM Check (ubuntu-latest)`
25	- `Release Artifact Preflight (macos-arm64)`
26	- `Release Artifact Preflight (linux-gnu)`
27	- `Release Artifact Preflight (linux-musl)`
28	- `Release Artifact Preflight (wasm-wasi)`
29	- `Validate Changesets & Workspace Status`
30	
31	The repository owner has an explicit ruleset bypass for emergency recovery. That bypass is not a
32	second approval mechanism and must be used only when the normal evidence path cannot run.
33	
34	## Release identity and recovery
35	
36	Every release run records two different revisions:
37	
38	- The orchestration revision: the workflow and Callisto CLI that coordinate the run.
39	- The release-source revision: the merged release commit whose exact versions are released.
40	
41	A recovery is a new run using current orchestration and an explicit full release-source SHA. It
42	does not rerun historical workflow code, create a version PR, or invent a newer version.
43	
44	The immutable run envelope and provider observations are recovery authority. A local state file
45	is useful crash evidence, but cannot prove what a registry, Git remote, or forge contains.
46	
47	The selected release profile is part of the immutable intent digest, not just a receipt label.
48	The production profile declares its GitHub forge destination in `callisto.toml`; planning rejects
49	an artifact repository that differs from that destination, and execution rejects a profile that
50	does not match its intent. An unconfigured profile fails before it writes an intent or dispatches
51	an effect.
52	
53	Each configured profile also declares `registry-routes`, mapping a logical package target such as
54	`cratesIo` to a concrete configured registry key. The resolved key and its credential-free
55	endpoint digest are part of the release operation and package fingerprint. A configured profile
56	cannot fall back to an un-routed production registry, and two profiles cannot share a forge or
57	configured registry destination.
58	
59	## Execution
60	
61	Before an effect, Callisto observes the provider. An operation is one of absent, exact success,
62	conflict, or indeterminate. Exact success becomes `AlreadySatisfied`; Callisto must not publish
63	the same version merely to learn whether it exists. Conflict and indeterminate observations fail
64	closed with an actionable diagnostic.
65	
66	The release succeeds only when every operation is provider-observed as exact success or already
67	satisfied. `Attempting`, failed, blocked, missing, and indeterminate are non-success states. A
68	receipt is emitted only after that global condition holds.
69	
70	## Workflow boundary
71	
72	GitHub Actions schedules jobs, supplies two isolated checkouts, transports artifacts, and injects
73	credentials only into execute. Callisto owns source validation, provenance, plan derivation,
74	provider observation, transition selection, resume, terminality, receipt creation, and artifact
75	validation. Workflow shell must not reimplement those semantics.
76	
77	All transient intent, state, downloaded artifacts, and build output live under `RUNNER_TEMP`, not
78	inside a source checkout. Build and plan have no registry credentials or provider-write token.
79	
80	## Product assets and rehearsal
81	
82	The product release will contain attested assets for `aarch64-apple-darwin`,
83	`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, and `wasm32-wasip1`. Apple signing and
84	notarization are intentionally out of scope until the project has a safe project-owned policy.
85	
86	Each asset's GitHub provenance is bound to the current coordinator workflow revision: that is the
87	revision GitHub records for the workflow run. The immutable intent and artifact manifest separately
88	bind those bytes to the selected release-source revision, so a recovery can safely use current
89	orchestration without misrepresenting an older source checkout as the workflow source.
90	
91	The private `orin-dx/callisto-rehearsal` forge repository is isolated from production. It is
92	reserved for future forge-level experiments; it is not a prerequisite for the current rehearsal.
93	
94	### Rehearsal boundary
95	
96	Callisto publishes Cargo crates to crates.io and product assets to GitHub Releases. It does not
97	publish to AWS, JFrog, GitHub Packages, or another registry merely to simulate a release.
98	
99	The hermetic provider harness is the rehearsal boundary until the project deliberately adopts an
100	isolated registry as a product requirement. It exercises the same CLI lifecycle, separate source
101	worktrees, provider observation, artifact validation, failure recovery, and fresh-runner state
102	reconstruction without publishing a package or introducing a second distribution service.
103	
104	The private `orin-dx/callisto-rehearsal` repository remains reserved for future forge-level
105	experiments. Do not add `[release.profiles.rehearsal]` or registry credentials while the product
106	has no isolated-registry requirement: a configured profile that cannot prove persistent provider
107	behavior would create false confidence rather than release safety.

content.text: Six read-only audit agents are running in parallel: core engine, config/CLI, workflow/CI, tests/coverage, architecture, and performance. The test agent is the only one allowed to run cargo, so the others won't contend for the build lock. I'll consolidate their findings when they report back.

FYI, this is what codex said:



<pasted_content id="087f">
  ### Material findings

  1. P1 — CLI can publish successfully, then reject the run and emit no receipt

     release execute performs all remote effects before parsing --orchestration-revision:
      - crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs:382
      - crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs:389

     A malformed revision, invalid receipt path, or later receipt failure can therefore leave crates/tags/releases published while the
     command exits unsuccessfully.

     Required black-box test:
      - pass an invalid orchestration SHA;
      - assert the command fails;
      - assert no fake provider effect occurred;
      - assert no partial state is reported as successful.

     Parse and validate all immutable run metadata and output paths before dispatching any operation.

  2. P1 — GitHub Release observation likely rejects real releases

     The implementation requires GitHub’s target_commitish to equal the release source SHA:
      - crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release.rs:1135

     But the workflow invokes gh release create ... --verify-tag without explicitly supplying a target commit. GitHub documents
     target_commitish as a branch/commitish field and examples commonly contain the default branch, such as master, not necessarily
     the tag’s commit SHA. GitHub Releases API (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/releases/releases)

     This is pre-existing in main, but PR #101 continues to depend on it, and artifact uploads now require the same release
     observation path. Add a real GitHub-compatible test fixture or change the identity check to use the immutable tag target, not
     target_commitish.

  3. P2 — Release reconciliation has poor scaling characteristics

     Every execution loop recomputes the entire transitive DAG:
      - crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs:74
      - crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs:264

     The DFS allocates/clones BTreeSet identities per operation. Since this runs after every operation, a long dependency chain can
     approach cubic work in the number of operations. Large monorepos will pay this cost during release execution.

     Add a benchmark/property test with hundreds or thousands of operations, then cache prerequisite closure or maintain incremental
     eligibility.

  4. P2 — Profile authority is split between CLI and graph layers

     The graph layer treats profile configuration as optional:
      - crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release.rs:1312

     The CLI separately validates the profile and artifact repository:
      - crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs:205

     This creates two semantic authorities. A caller of the public graph API can construct an intent with an arbitrary profile/
     artifact policy relationship that the domain model does not reject. The graph should resolve a profile into a typed destination
     binding and enforce that binding during intent construction and validation.

  ### Coverage gaps

  The current black-box suite covers the main happy path, recovery, partial publication, and artifact filtering well, but is missing:

  - invalid orchestration SHA with assertion of zero provider effects;
  - receipt-directory creation/write failures after successful effects;
  - GitHub API 401, 403, 429, 500, malformed JSON, duplicate assets, and missing asset digests;
  - failed gh attestation verify;
  - profile/forge mismatch during execution;
  - profile registry-route changes between planning and execution;
  - large-DAG performance;
  - real GitHub Release target_commitish behavior;
  - recovery with missing state plus an Absent observation for every operation;
  - non-recovery execution with missing state and pre-existing remote effects.

  The existing provider fake also treats attestation verification as unconditional success, so it does not exercise the most security-
  sensitive artifact failure path.

  just fmt-check passes. The broader test invocations were blocked behind the shared Cargo build lock and were interrupted; I would
  not treat the PR’s reported CI count as closing the cases above.
</pasted_content id="087f">

  - Only the test fake at `durable_release_e2e_tests.rs:518` hard-codes the commit SHA. So the first real publish would create the GitHub Release and then fail as a `Conflict`, and no test can catch it.
  - The check was introduced in `eeda4a2f` (#39) and is not new in this PR, but this PR's artifact uploads depend on it. I'd treat it as P0 for the first real release.

The performance audit is back. At Callisto scale (about 9 crates, 31 operations, 4 artifacts) there is no algorithmic hotspot, so Codex #3 is real but low priority. Three agents are still running (workflow/CI, tests, architecture).

**Codex #3 (DAG re-closure cost).** I checked the code (`release_execution.rs:291-313`). `visited.remove(id)` on exit turns the DFS into path enumeration, which is exponential on dense layered DAGs, not just cubic. Callisto's real DAG is about 370 visits per pass, so it doesn't matter today. Codex's suggested fix is right: a single topological pass.

**New release-blocking candidate (X1).** `recheck_trust` (`release.rs:214`) compares the whole `GitCommitTrustEvidence` with `!=`, and that type derives `PartialEq` over `allowed_ignored_paths`. The agent reports that a real `cargo publish` creates `release-source/target/`. Git status then shows `!! target/`, the next recheck sees changed evidence, and the run aborts with `ReleaseIntentStale` after the first crate. It simulated this in a scratch clone, but I have only confirmed the comparison and the derive, not the `target/` side effect. The e2e fake `cargo publish` touches a marker outside the worktree, so no test can catch it.

**Other performance findings:**
- **No timeouts.** Most outbound calls, including `git push`, `gh release create` and `upload`, both `gh api` calls and `cargo publish`, have no timeout, and no workflow job has `timeout-minutes`. One hang holds the release concurrency group for up to 6 hours.
- **Discarded rate-limit data.** Rate-limit and transient errors are classified and then discarded. Each one leaves the operation `Attempting` and needs a full recovery run.
- **Recovery is slow.** Recovery also pays the full serial `verify` job, checked against main's tip rather than the release source. A flaky unrelated test can block recovery of a half-published release.
- **Serial CI setup.** The critical path builds a debug `callisto` and installs the toolchain six times in series, and installs `cross` from source on every run.
- **Redundant provider calls.** Observation is repeated and uncached, at about 12 identical GETs per release for 4 asset slots. That is small at this scale.

Correction to the license finding: it is a stale-base artifact, and I'm withdrawing it. The PR branch is two commits behind `main`. `#100` (`50517d8d`) already moved the manifests to `FSL-1.1-MIT` and `MIT`, and this PR's `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and README edits bring the docs in line with that. I simulated the merge and it is clean, with manifests, `LICENSE`, README and `AGENTS.md` all consistent. Three agents flagged it because they read the PR head, so my earlier "settle it before first publish" was wrong.

- Fix the concurrency loss: a pending release run can be replaced.
- Stop a pending changeset from suppressing a release.
- Recovery must not be blocked by an unrelated `verify` failure.
- Add a PR dry-run rehearsal (plan, build, attest, manifest).
- Verify or drop the unverified installer; pin the transitive action.

**Cross-cutting tests, landing with each phase:**
- A provider contract tier.
- A **model-based fault-injection simulator**: crash at every persistence point and inject every provider outcome. Invariants: no success with a non-terminal operation, no duplicate publish, convergence within k recoveries, no receipt without fresh exact evidence.
- E-code assertions instead of substring checks.
- The parsed-YAML checker.
- A spec-to-test traceability check (every SRL criterion must map to a named test).

**Phase 5: hygiene and delivery.** One spec location. Redact the incident report, or move it out of the public repo. Fix the docs that contradict the code (`ARCHITECTURE.md` still says "release Environment"; `docs/06` example commands lack required flags). A complete changeset. Split into PRs: hygiene, model+graph, config+CLI, workflow+docs.

**Release gate.** The first real release happens only when the contract tier, the simulator and a full dry-run rehearsal are green.

**Process.** A `scribe:architect` spec for Phases 1–2, exit-gated, then `navigator` and `smith` run sequentially with targeted tests after each fix. Reviewers must run the commands themselves. Decisions the owner hasn't made get marked as judgment calls, per the incident memory.

## Decisions I need from you

1. **Observation architecture.** (a) Observe through the profile-bound registry endpoint over HTTP, with a hermetic local protocol server for tests. That gives real protocol semantics inside the current rehearsal boundary, and is my recommendation. (b) Keep shelling to `cargo`, `gh` and `git`, with the contract tier only.
2. **Scope of `[release]`.** Generic and data-driven (recommended), or explicitly self-release-only.
3. **GitHub Release flow.** Draft, upload, then publish, with `--prerelease` for prerelease versions (recommended).
4. **Sources without `[release]`.** How should `0e0016ed` (0.7.2) be recovered? Options: a repair commit as the incident plan allows, or make plan tolerate absent artifact flags.
5. **Recovery gating.** Should recovery skip `verify`, given its time-varying audit?
6. **Delivery.** Restructure this PR into the four PRs, or keep one.

## Verification status

- **Confirmed by me:**
  - The three P0s: I re-ran `gh api --repo` and `cargo info` against the workspace, and checked live `target_commitish` values.
  - Codex #1: argument validation runs after effects.
  - Codex #2: the `target_commitish` mismatch.

  - The stale-base retention-days mix.

content.text:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

**Adjusted plan: four tracks, six sequential workflows.** Build steps run strictly one at a time. Parallelism is used only for reading, falsifying and judging. Nothing has been launched. The plan is estimates and structure only, and it starts on your go-ahead.

## Cost and quality rules

1. **Use each plugin agent's built-in tier via `agentType`, and override only where noted.** Their frontmatter already encodes the trade-off:
   - Haiku/low: recon and commit messages.
   - Sonnet/medium: implementers, reviewers, auditors, planners, mutators.
   - Opus/high: every exit-gate and `ranger:adversary`.
   - Fable 5.1/high: `scribe:architect` and `scribe:arch-auditor`.
   - I haven't confirmed that a workflow's `agentType` honours that frontmatter model, so the first workflow includes a one-call smoke check.
2. **Breadth cheap, depth on demand.** Sonnet skeptics and auditors do the wide work. Opus adjudicates only disagreements and issues one binding gate per batch.
3. **Escalation ladder.** Sonnet, then after two failed review loops one Opus/high retry, then stop and ask you.
4. **No parallel builds and no worktree isolation.** Each worktree needs its own `target/` and a cold rebuild, and your memory notes say parallel fixing fails on coupled code. Exactly one agent, or I, owns cargo at a time, using `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=<empty>` for the gpgsign hang.
5. **Spec ceremony only for structural work.** Targeted fixes use the RED tests as their criteria, and gate rounds are capped at 2 (your canon-loop memory).
6. **Deterministic checks are mine.** I run scoped cargo and `just ci-fast` at every batch gate. Reviewers must paste real command output.
7. **Hand off by file path and JSON schema.** Specs go in `.claude/specs`, plans in `.claude/plans`.
8. **Foreground discipline.** One workflow at a time. I read each result before the next, falling back to `journal.jsonl` if a notification looks stale.
9. **Provenance tags.** Every spec criterion is marked owner requirement, existing contract, external constraint, or judgment call. Judgment calls pause for your acceptance (the incident rule).

## Tracks

- **S, structural, spec-driven, sequential.** RunEnvelope and canonical types, then the state machine and observation model, then the provider port and executor (with the contract tier and fault-injection simulator built as tasks), then the CLI typestate and `release candidate`/`matrix`.
- **T, targeted, RED-test-driven, no spec.** Workflow adapter fixes, config canonicalization, timeouts, YAML policy checker, installer.
- **H, hygiene, no cargo, parallel-safe.** Rebase, docs that are wrong today, incident report redaction, changeset. Behaviour docs wait until after T.
- **A, assurance.** Independent audit, mutation and gates. It builds nothing.

## Workflows

| # | Purpose | Agents (tier) | Exit |
|---|---|---|---|
| W0 | Truth and RED baseline | `smith:recon` (Haiku/low). About 8 Sonnet skeptics, one per unverified claim (X1, PyPI dispatch, tag-template/installer, recovery of `0e0016ed`, historic rerun, yanked crates, attestation binding), each reproducing with real tools. Opus adjudicates disputes only. One `smith:implementer` (Sonnet) places the 34 proposed tests as RED, plus real-tool repros. | Every defect has a failing test or is struck. |
| W1 | Design: 3 specs (envelope/state, provider port/executor, execute typestate/candidate) | `scribe:architect` ×3 in sequence for consistency (Fable/high). Then per spec, in parallel: `scribe:auditor` and `scribe:verifier` (Sonnet), plus `vanguard:risk-assessor` on the port spec. One `scribe:arch-auditor` (Fable/high) across all three. `scribe:drafter` fixes (Sonnet). `scribe:exit-gate` per spec (Opus/high), max 2 rounds. | **Pause: you accept the judgment calls.** |
| W2 | Plan | `navigator:planner` ×3, `challenger` ×3 (Sonnet), one cross-plan Opus/high challenger for ordering and sibling interfaces. Planner flags `hard` tasks. Estimator skipped. | You see the plan and a refined cost estimate. |
| W3 | Build S, batches: model, graph, CLI | Per task: `smith:implementer` (Sonnet/medium; Opus/high only for the roughly 3 `hard` tasks: state machine, port and executor loop, trust-evidence split), then `smith:reviewer` (Sonnet), then at most 2 fix loops. At each batch end: `smith:mutator` (Sonnet), survivors become tests, `smith:exit-gate` (Opus/high), and I run cargo. | Batch gate green. |
| W4 | Build T | Same loop, no spec. Haiku/low for mechanical edits (retention, `timeout-minutes`, dropped secrets, docs). Sonnet for the YAML policy checker and installer. | Gate green. |
| W5 | Assurance | `ranger:audit` on the final diff: recon (Haiku), scanner and boundary-tracer (Sonnet), `adversary` per candidate and exit-gate (Opus/high). `bug-hunter` (Sonnet) covers YAML and shell, which ranger doesn't. `sentinel:gate` last. I run the simulator on more seeds and `just ci`. | Release gate. |
| W6 | Delivery | `courier` commit-analyzer (Haiku), changeset-analyzer and pr-narrator (Sonnet). | PRs drafted. |

Track H runs alongside W0 to W2.

**Rough scale (estimate).** About 130 to 170 agent calls, roughly 80% Sonnet/medium and the rest Opus, Fable and Haiku. I'll report actuals after each workflow and refine at W2. If you give a `+Nk` token directive, it becomes a hard ceiling for the workflows.

## Stop-and-ask points

- After W0, with the defect ledger.
- After W1, for the judgment calls.
- After W2, with the plan and estimate.
- Any batch where the exit-gate fails twice.
- Before any commit, push, PR, or dispatch of the dry-run rehearsal (outward-facing). Implementers run with `commit_authorized: false` until you say otherwise.

## Still needed from you (Gate 0)

Your six decisions from the earlier plan, plus two new ones. Defaults if you say "go with recommendations":

1. **Observation.** HTTP endpoint with a hermetic protocol server for registries.
2. **`[release]` scope.** Generic and data-driven.
3. **GitHub Release flow.** Draft, upload, then publish, with `--prerelease` for prereleases.
4. **Recovery of `0e0016ed`.** Plan tolerates the artifact flags when the source has no `[release]`, and releases crates only, with an explicit notice.
5. **Recovery gating.** Skip the full `verify`; run the targeted checks only.
6. **Delivery.** Stacked PRs: hygiene, model+graph, config+CLI, workflow+docs.
7. **Commits.** Local per-task commits via `courier`, held until you review, and no pushes.
8. **Outward actions.** Whether I may dispatch the dry-run rehearsal on GitHub and open the stacked PRs (each still asks first).
Let's fire it up and build on top of the PR branch please

    { title: 'Baseline', detail: 'build one debug callisto binary and record the baseline', model: 'haiku' },
    { title: 'Falsify', detail: 'one skeptic per unverified claim; Opus adjudicates only non-confirmed', model: 'sonnet' },
    { title: 'RED suite', detail: 'place proposed tests and real-tool repros as ignored RED tests', model: 'sonnet' },

}

const REPO = '/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto'
const SCRATCH = '/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-callisto/a08620cc-8b37-45b5-b4b2-89a977aad490/scratchpad'
const EMPTY_GITCONFIG = SCRATCH + '/empty-gitconfig'
const AUDIT = REPO + '/.claude/plans/PR101-HARDENING'

const COMMON_RULES = [
  'Repository: ' + REPO + ' at HEAD 562957b0 (PR 101 head 4d05e40d merged with main). Full audit reports are in ' + AUDIT + '/audit/ (pr101-core.md, pr101-config-cli.md, pr101-workflow.md, pr101-tests.md, pr101-arch.md, pr101-perf.md); read only what you need.',
  'Set GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=' + EMPTY_GITCONFIG + ' on every git or cargo command (the global gpgsign config hangs test fixtures).',
  'NEVER edit tracked files unless your task says so. NEVER run git commit, git push, git checkout -- Cargo.lock, or anything that publishes or writes to a remote.',
  'Report only what you observed. Quote file:line for code claims and paste real command output for behaviour claims. Do not infer a result you did not observe.',
].join('\n')

const BASELINE_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    head: { type: 'string' },
    tracked_clean: { type: 'boolean' },
    binary: { type: 'string' },

}

const CLAIM_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    id: { type: 'string' },
    verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['confirmed', 'refuted', 'inconclusive'] },
    severity_if_confirmed: { type: 'string', enum: ['P0', 'P1', 'P2', 'P3'] },

const CLAIMS = [
  {
    id: 'C1-trust-recheck-target-dir',
    title: 'cargo publish dirties the release-source worktree and trips recheck_trust',
    statement: 'recheck_trust (crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release.rs ~214-233) compares the whole GitCommitTrustEvidence with != , including allowed_ignored_paths (crates/callisto-vcs/src/access.rs ~38-44) that come from git status --ignored=matching (crates/callisto-vcs/src/shell.rs). Real cargo publish (crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/registry_argv.rs ~68-73, no --no-verify) creates target/package under the source root, so after the first crate publishes, the next recheck (release_execution.rs ~77) sees different evidence and aborts with ReleaseIntentStale.',
    how: 'In a scratch git repo with one tiny crate and NO CARGO_TARGET_DIR, run real cargo package or cargo publish --dry-run --allow-dirty and show git status --ignored=matching --porcelain before and after. Read how allowed_ignored_paths is built and whether target/ is in the allowlist and therefore recorded. Grep .github for CARGO_TARGET_DIR. Confirm or refute that the evidence values differ before/after.',
  },
  {
    id: 'C2-pypi-nuget-registry-paths',
    title: 'PyPI is unobservable but still uploads; non-default registries regress for non-self users',
    statement: 'For Ecosystem::Pypi the release observation returns Indeterminate (release.rs ~507) while dispatch_registry (~599-624) still runs the upload, so a PyPI package could publish irreversibly and then never yield a receipt.   },
  {
    id: 'C3-cli-tag-template-and-installer',
    title: 'callisto-cli tag template changed to callisto@{version}; installer and last-tag lookup do not follow',
    statement: 'callisto.toml (new [[package]] block) sets tag-template callisto@{version} for cargo/callisto-cli. Existing tags are callisto-cli@0.4.0 to 0.5.0. The npm classifier (~434-441) does the same.',

Result: a manifest naming any source_commit validates, and nothing binds artifact bytes to the release source except the coordinator attestation.',
    how: 'Trace with quoted lines. Then write (in the scratchpad, not in the repo) the smallest model-level test sketch that would fail today, and state precisely which fields it constructs.',
  },
  {
    id: 'C7-attempting-before-observation',
    title: 'Attempting is persisted before pre-effect observation and wedges the operation',
    statement: 'release_execution.rs (~78-83) persists Attempting then dispatch_prepared observes (release.rs ~565, 808, 865, 922). After the operator fixes the cause, recover_interrupted (~163-184) demands an Exact observation, and Absent returns ReleaseRecoveryUnresolved (do not retry) until the state file is deleted.',
    how: 'Trace with quoted lines and, if feasible with the built binary and a scratch fixture using fake cargo/gh on PATH (see crates/callisto-cli/tests/durable_release_e2e_tests.rs for the fake provider technique), demonstrate: first run fails before any effect, second run with the cause fixed still refuses with the recovery-unresolved diagnostic.',
  },
  {
    id: 'C8-shared-destination-check',
    title: 'Shared-destination isolation check has a false positive and spelling bypasses',
    statement: 'crates/callisto-graph/src/config/resolve.rs (~180-194, 615-640) rejects two profiles that both leave a route unset (Option None == None) or route different logical keys, compares raw registry url strings (bypass with host case, default port, trailing slash), and GitHubRepository (crates/callisto-model/src/release.rs ~167-169, 262-269) derives Eq on raw strings (bypass with owner case or a .git suffix; dot and dot-dot components parse). A single non-production profile routing cratesIo to cratesIo is also accepted.',
    how: 'Use the built binary in scratch workspaces with crafted callisto.toml [release] sections and run a config-loading command (for example status). Show accept/reject for each of the five cases.',

  [
    'Establish the baseline for a hardening effort. Do exactly this and nothing else:',

phase('Falsify')
const skepticPrompt = (c) => [
  'You are a skeptic-reproducer for ONE audit claim about PR 101 of Callisto. Your job is to try to REPRODUCE the claim with real tools and observed output, and report honestly, including when it does not hold.',
  '',
  'CLAIM ' + c.id + ': ' + c.title,
  c.statement,
  '',
  'HOW TO CONFIRM: ' + c.how,
  '',
  'Environment: a debug callisto binary is at ' + base.binary + ' (built from HEAD). Work in scratch directories under ' + SCRATCH + '/w0/' + c.id + '/ . You may run cargo ONLY inside scratch fixture repos with their own CARGO_TARGET_DIR under that scratch directory; do NOT run cargo build, test or clippy against ' + REPO + ' (another stage owns its build lock). Network reads (gh api GET, cargo info) are allowed; nothing may publish, push, tag or write to any remote.',
  'Verdict rules: confirmed only if you observed the failure (pasted output) or, for pure code-path claims, traced it with quoted file:line. refuted if the code or a real run contradicts the claim (say what actually happens). inconclusive if you could not settle it; say what is missing.',

  '',
  'CLAIM ' + c.id + ': ' + c.title,

  '',

].join('\n')

const results = await pipeline(
  CLAIMS,
  (c) => agent(skepticPrompt(c), { label: 'skeptic:' + c.id, phase: 'Falsify', agentType: 'bug-hunter', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'medium', schema: CLAIM_SCHEMA }),
  (first, c) => {
    if (first && first.verdict === 'confirmed') return first
    log('Escalating ' + c.id + ' to adjudication (skeptic verdict: ' + (first ? first.verdict : 'no result') + ')')
    return agent(adjudicatorPrompt(c, first), { label: 'adjudicate:' + c.id, phase: 'Falsify', agentType: 'bug-hunter', model: 'opus', effort: 'high', schema: CLAIM_SCHEMA })
  },
)

const ledger = CLAIMS.map((c, i) => ({ claim: c.id, title: c.title, result: results[i] || null }))
const confirmed = ledger.filter((l) => l.result && l.result.verdict === 'confirmed')
log('Falsification: ' + confirmed.length + ' of ' + CLAIMS.length + ' claims confirmed; ' + ledger.filter((l) => !l.result || l.result.verdict !== 'confirmed').map((l) => l.claim).join(', ') + ' not confirmed.')

phase('RED suite')
const DEFECTS = [
  'D01 (P0, live-verified): cargo_version_is_published runs "cargo info name@ver" with cwd = the workspace root (release.rs ~781-799), so cargo resolves the local manifest, prints "from ./crates/..." and exits 0 for an unpublished version; --registry is only added when the key is not cratesIo. Contract test: fake cargo logs cwd and argv; assert the info invocation runs outside any Cargo workspace and names the registry explicitly (crates-io).',
  'D02 (P0, live-verified): gh api is invoked with --repo (release.rs ~997-1006 and ~1108-1118) but gh api has no --repo flag (gh 2.101.0: "unknown flag: --repo"). Contract test: a strict fake gh that rejects unknown flags like the real one for the api subcommand, plus (skipped at runtime when gh is absent) a check that every flag we emit appears in real "gh api --help".',
  'D03 (P0, live-verified): forge Exact requires target_commitish == source SHA (release.rs ~1144-1145) but GitHub returns the default branch name ("main") for a release created by gh release create --verify-tag without --target (dispatch_forge_release ~879-887); the existing fake gh hard-codes the SHA (durable_release_e2e_tests.rs ~518). Test: fake gh returns a real-shaped release object with target_commitish "main"; a normal release run and a recovery run must still succeed and upload assets.',
  'D04 (P1, mechanism traced): a real cargo publish leaves target/ in the source worktree; recheck_trust compares allowed_ignored_paths and aborts the next operation with ReleaseIntentStale. Test: the fake cargo publish creates target/package/x inside its cwd like real cargo does; a two-crate release must complete. Also a contract test (temp git repo, real cargo package, skipped if cargo is unavailable) proving real cargo creates target/ under the source directory.',
  'D05 (P1, probed): release execute parses --orchestration-revision only after all effects (cli release.rs ~382-394). Test p06 in the proposed tests.',
  'D06 (P1, probed): with no [release] section, --profile does-not-exist plans and executes against the production registry (cli release.rs ~243-250, ~340; graph ~1312-1316, ~1801-1815). Test p08 in the proposed tests.',
  'D07 (P2, probed): a bare product-package (no ecosystem) is accepted and silently derives zero artifact slots (config/resolve.rs ~153-156; graph ~1537). Graph config test 6c in the proposed tests.',
  'D08 (P1, probed): tag observation reads only local refs (release.rs ~1048-1100); a tag created locally whose push failed is treated as Exact/AlreadySatisfied on rerun. Test with a REAL git bare remote (file:// remote) and fake cargo/gh: pre-create the local tag without pushing, rerun, and assert the tag is pushed to the remote and the receipt is only issued after the remote has it.',
].join('\n')

const ledgerText = ledger
  .filter((l) => l.result && l.result.verdict === 'confirmed')
  .map((l) => l.claim + ' [' + (l.result.severity_if_confirmed || '?') + '] ' + l.title + '\n  red test: ' + (l.result.red_test_crate || '?') + ' :: ' + (l.result.red_test_name || '?') + '\n  sketch: ' + l.result.red_test_sketch)
  .join('\n')

const implementerPrompt = (feedback) => [
  'You are implementing the RED baseline for a Callisto hardening effort. Goal: every audited defect gets a deterministic failing black-box test that is parked as ignored, so the branch stays green while the defects are provably captured, and the not-yet-failing proposed tests become normal regression tests.',
  '',
  'INPUTS',
  '- Proposed tests already drafted and verified to compile against HEAD (23 CLI tests: 19 pass, 4 fail; 5 model tests pass; 6 graph config tests: 5 pass, 1 fails): ' + AUDIT + '/proposed-tests/ . The audit report ' + AUDIT + '/audit/pr101-tests.md section 6 and 7 explains each test (p01-p21) and which ones fail on HEAD.',
  '- Defects to capture (D01-D08):\n' + DEFECTS,
  '- Additional defects confirmed by independent falsification in this run (add a RED test for each; skip any that has no sketch):\n' + (ledgerText || '(none)'),
  '',
  'RULES',
  '1. Tests must be BLACK BOX: drive the compiled binary or public API, assert exit codes, typed diagnostic codes (E-codes), files and recorded provider effects. No private helpers, no source greps. Where an error has a typed code, assert the code, not prose.',
  '2. A test that passes on HEAD is a normal test. A test that fails on HEAD because of a captured defect is named with the prefix red_d<NN>_ (or red_c<N>_ for a falsification claim) and marked #[ignore = "DEFECT-<ID>: <one short line>"]. It must fail for the stated reason, not because of a compile, setup or fixture error: run it with --ignored and read the failure output.',
  '3. Shared fixture code: do not paste a second copy of the 500-line fake-provider harness. Check crates/callisto-cli/tests/common/ and durable_release_e2e_tests.rs; move the reusable fake cargo/gh/git helpers into crates/callisto-cli/tests/common/ (or the existing convention) and have both files use them WITHOUT changing the behaviour of the existing durable_release_e2e_tests. The existing 11 tests must still pass unchanged.',
  '4. The fake provider tools must model the real tools: fake gh rejects unknown flags for api and release, fake cargo logs cwd and argv, fake git push is real git against a bare file:// remote where D08 needs it. Keep the old permissive behaviour only where existing tests rely on it, via an explicit opt-in.',
  '5. Add a just recipe release-red that runs only the parked tests: cargo test with -- --ignored red_ for the three crates. Add .github/tests/verify-no-open-defects.sh that fails while any #[ignore = "DEFECT-" remains; do NOT wire either into just ci or CI yet.',

  '',

].join('\n')

  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    files_changed: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    tests: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          file: { type: 'string' },
          name: { type: 'string' },
          status: { type: 'string', enum: ['normal', 'parked'] },
          defect: { type: 'string' },
          failure_reason: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['file', 'name', 'status'],
      },
    },
    existing_e2e_still_passes: { type: 'boolean' },
    notes: { type: 'string' },
  },
  required: ['files_changed', 'tests', 'existing_e2e_still_passes'],
}

const REVIEW_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    green_suite_ok: { type: 'boolean' },
    green_evidence: { type: 'string' },
    parked: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          test: { type: 'string' },
          failed_when_run: { type: 'boolean' },
          fails_for_stated_reason: { type: 'boolean' },
          evidence: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['test', 'failed_when_run', 'fails_for_stated_reason', 'evidence'],
      },
    },
    unparked_defects: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    production_code_touched: { type: 'boolean' },
    problems: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    approved: { type: 'boolean' },
  },
  required: ['green_suite_ok', 'parked', 'production_code_touched', 'problems', 'approved'],
}

let red = await agent(implementerPrompt(''), { label: 'implement-red', phase: 'RED suite', agentType: 'smith:implementer', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'medium', schema: RED_SCHEMA })
if (!red) {
  log('RED implementer returned no result.')
  return { aborted: true, base, ledger }
}

phase('Review')
let review = null
for (let round = 1; round <= 3; round++) {
  review = await agent(
    [
      'You are the independent reviewer of a RED-baseline change in ' + REPO + '. You did not write it. Your value is that you actually RUN things and read the output; a prior review agent once falsely reported a check as clean without running it, so every claim you make must be backed by pasted command output.',
      '',
      'The implementer reports: ' + JSON.stringify(red),
      '',
      'Do all of this (you are the only agent allowed to run cargo against the workspace now; per-crate only; GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=' + EMPTY_GITCONFIG + '):',
      '1. git diff --stat and git status --short: confirm NO production code under crates/*/src changed (test-only changes under tests/ and #[cfg(test)] plus justfile and .github/tests are allowed). Set production_code_touched accordingly.',
      '2. Run the normal (non-ignored) tests of every touched crate: cargo test -p callisto-cli, and -p callisto-model / -p callisto-graph if their tests changed. Report real pass/fail counts. green_suite_ok only if zero failures.',
      '3. Run the parked tests: cargo test -p <crate> -- --ignored red_ . For EACH parked test confirm it fails, and read the failure output to decide whether it fails for the stated defect (the assertion that fires matches the defect) rather than a fixture, compile or environment error. Be strict: a RED test failing for the wrong reason must be reported as a problem.',
      '4. Check every defect D01-D08 and every confirmed falsification claim has a parked test; list any missing in unparked_defects. Defects list:\n' + DEFECTS,
      '5. Check black-box quality: flag any test that asserts on prose substrings where a typed E-code exists, reaches private helpers, or duplicates the shared harness.',
      '6. approved only if green_suite_ok, no production code touched, every parked test fails for its stated reason, no defect is missing, and problems is empty.',
      '',
      COMMON_RULES,
    ].join('\n'),
    { label: 'review-red-round-' + round, phase: 'Review', agentType: 'smith:reviewer', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'medium', schema: REVIEW_SCHEMA },
  )
  if (review && review.approved) break
  if (round === 3 || !review) break
  log('Review round ' + round + ' found problems: ' + review.problems.join(' | '))
  const fixed = await agent(
    implementerPrompt(JSON.stringify({ problems: review.problems, unparked_defects: review.unparked_defects, parked: review.parked.filter((p) => !p.fails_for_stated_reason) })),
    { label: 'fix-red-round-' + round, phase: 'RED suite', agentType: 'smith:implementer', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'medium', schema: RED_SCHEMA },
  )
  if (fixed) red = fixed
}

return { base, ledger, red, review }

**No, it isn't going as planned.** W0 is about two hours in against my guess of well under an hour. It is still making progress, so I'm leaving it running.

**Timeline (from the workflow journal):**
- **Baseline: about 60 minutes.** This was a cold debug build after the merge, and the e2e test binary took a long time to compile. The Haiku agent also thrashed: it killed and restarted its own builds several times.
- **Falsify: about 2 minutes.** It confirmed all 8 claims. That is fast and unanimous, so I spot-checked C4 and C1. Both had real evidence: C4 ran the actual plan command against `0e0016ed` and captured the rejection, and C1 traced the allowlist code and ran a real scratch-repo cargo run. No Opus escalation was needed. I'll still skim the rest of the evidence before trusting the ledger.
- **RED suite: about 58 minutes so far.** The implementer has made 56 Bash calls, and each cargo cycle takes about 5 minutes. It is actively iterating: a test run started at 15:11 is still going, so it isn't hung. It also created several new integration test files (`release_hardening_tests`, `release_plan_pypi_default_registry_test`, `cli_tag_template`, and others), and each file is a separate binary that must be compiled and linked, which adds to the cycle time.

**Estimate for the rest:** the implementer needs perhaps 15 to 30 more minutes. The reviewer then re-runs the crate suites plus the parked tests, likely another 20 to 40 minutes. Low confidence on both.

**Problem to know about:** the baseline agent ran `pkill -9 rustc`, which kills every rustc process on the machine. That could have killed builds in your other sessions if any were running (I saw peer sessions listed earlier). Worth a look if something died around 14:12 local time. I hadn't said "don't kill processes" in the workflow prompt, and I'll add that rule to every later one.

**Changes for the next workflows:**
- Have the implementer batch into one integration test binary instead of many. That cuts link time.
- Run `cargo test --no-run` once, then run only targeted tests.
- Have me run the heavy gates rather than paying for two agents to repeat them.
- Set a wall-clock limit per stage.
- Forbid killing processes the agent didn't start.

content.text:
**You're right that this shouldn't take hours, and I found a likely cause.** It isn't the machine: 12 cores, load about 3, 162 GB free.

**What I measured:**
- **Feature sets flip between runs.** Different `-p` selections resolve different feature sets for shared dependencies, so cargo rebuilds them. I compared `cargo tree` for `callisto-cli`, `callisto-graph`, and `callisto-model + callisto-graph`, and the sets differ for `serde_core`, `rustix`, `futures-executor`, `getrandom` and `regex-syntax`.
- **The heavy rebuilds follow.** `serde_core` sits at the bottom of the tree, so a change there invalidates everything above it, including the `gix-*` crates. When I looked, rustc was live-compiling `gix_status`, `gix_merge` and `gix_blame`. The agents alternate `-p callisto-cli` and `-p callisto-model -p callisto-graph`, and each switch rebuilds a big slice of the tree. The audit agents did the same before, which fits the earlier 9 to 17 minute waits.
- **Not yet timed.** I haven't run a timed A/B, because the implementer holds the cargo lock now. I'd rate this as a strong explanation, not proven.
- **Right now** the implementer's `cargo test -p callisto-model -p callisto-graph ...` has been running for 11 minutes.

**On building and testing only at the end:** I'd keep some verification in the loop. Compiling and running tests is the only thing that proves a RED test fails for the stated reason, and if every failure surfaces at once, several will share the same cause. I'd change the cadence instead:

1. **One cargo invocation shape, always.** Use `cargo test --workspace` with test-name filters, so features never flip. The first run is cold. After that it is incremental.
2. **`cargo check` inside tasks, tests at gates.** Agents only compile-check while writing. I run the full workspace test at batch gates, not agents. That is close to your suggestion without losing the RED/GREEN proof.
3. **Fewer test binaries.** Put new tests in one integration binary. This W0 created many, and each one is a separate link.
4. **Permanent fix later:** a `workspace-hack` crate (cargo-hakari) makes every package selection resolve identical features. I'd propose it as its own small PR.
5. **Guardrails.** No process killing, and a wall-clock limit per stage.

**Decision for the running W0:** the implementer is probably near the end, but the reviewer stage will repeat the same alternation.
- **(a)** Let it finish. My guess is another 30 to 60 minutes.
- **(b)** Stop after the implementer's current cargo run and have me verify with one `cargo test --workspace` invocation, replacing the reviewer agent. The implementer's edits stay on disk, so nothing is lost.

I recommend (b). Say which and I'll proceed. I'll also time the A/B (`-p callisto-cli`, then `-p callisto-model -p callisto-graph`, then `-p callisto-cli` again) once the lock frees, so we know the actual saving.
Can we wrap this up quicker please?

content.text:
W0 is done: I stopped the slow reviewer stage and verified the RED suite myself in one cargo run. The commit message is being drafted now, and I'll commit locally without pushing.

**Results:**
- **Falsification.** All 8 audit claims were confirmed with real evidence.
- **Suite passes.** The normal tests pass (exit 0): the 11 existing e2e tests unchanged, 21 new hardening tests, 5 new config tests, and 5 new model tests.
- **Defects captured.** 22 parked `red_*` tests all fail when run with `--ignored`. I read each failure message, and they match the stated defects:
  - **D01:** `cargo info` runs inside the workspace.
  - **D02:** `--repo` is rejected by both the strict fake `gh` and the real `gh api --help`.
  - **D03:** E167, the forge release isn't observed after creation, with a permissive `gh`, so the cause is isolated.
  - **D04:** E124, the trust evidence changes after `cargo publish`.
  - **D05:** the orchestration revision is validated after effects.
  - **D06 and D07:** the unconfigured profile without `[release]`, and the bare `product-package`.
  - **D08:** a receipt is issued although the remote never received the tag.
  - **Falsification claims C2, C3, C6, C7, C8:** covered, with 5 isolation-bypass tests for C8.
- **Test harness.** The shared fake-provider harness now has an opt-in strict `gh` that rejects unknown flags, and a knob for the real `target_commitish` shape. The old permissive behaviour stays the default so existing tests are unchanged.

**Gaps and open items:**
- **Missing tests.** Two claims have no parked test yet, because the implementer was cut off: C4 (recovery of a source without `[release]`) and C5 (yanked or already-published crates).
- **Clippy.** I haven't run `just lint` on the new test code. `cargo fmt` was failing on the new files, and I fixed it.
- **Startup delay unexplained.** The tests themselves run in about 12 seconds, but each new test binary took about a minute before starting, roughly 7 minutes of unexplained wall-clock. Re-running the same binaries took 6 seconds in total. I refuted two hypotheses: a fresh 1.2 MB test-binary copy started in 0.1 seconds, and a fresh copy of the large `callisto` binary in 0.5 seconds. It's unexplained, and I'll time each stage next run instead of guessing.
- **Build time.** The cold build in the single `-p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph -p callisto-model` shape took 9m16s. Later runs should be incremental.

**Next:** W1 (design specs) has no cargo dependency except my gates, so it will run fast. Before that I'll add C4 and C5 tests as a small task, unless you'd rather fold them into the design work.

**W1 didn't pass: all three specs failed the exit gate after two correction rounds.** They are written but not accepted. It took 24 agents, 69 minutes and about 2.7M tokens. The specs are in `.claude/specs/`, untracked, and the owner-call list is in the scratchpad (`w1-owner-calls.json`).

| Spec | Criteria | Gate blockers |
|---|---|---|
| `SPEC-RELEASE-ENVELOPE-STATE` (A) | 27 | 4 |
| `SPEC-RELEASE-PROVIDER-EXECUTOR` (B) | 23 | 4 |
| `SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTE-SURFACE` (C) | 30 | 6 |

The blockers fall into three groups:
1. **Scope.** All three are too big for one planning cycle. B admitted this itself and proposed a B1/B2/B3 split.
2. **Cross-spec contradictions.** The main one is what happens when a version already exists in an initial run (no `--recover` flag). A says `AlreadySatisfied`. B says `Blocked`, which contradicts the existing SRL-07 contract that an exact pre-existing effect is recorded as already satisfied. C and A also disagree on which registry keys the built-in coverage test iterates, and two specs both claim `is_managed_release_branch`.
3. **Provenance tags.** Five criteria are mislabelled, for example a `[UR]` tag on an item that is really a judgment call.

The gate is right about the scope, and more correction rounds won't fix it, since that is the loop your canon-pipeline notes warn about. The remedy is to slice the work, not to gate harder.

**Recommendation**
1. **Resolve the three contradictions in one targeted pass.** Adopt A's semantics (`AlreadySatisfied` on initial runs, `Adopted` on recovery runs). Fix the tags. Keep the specs `proposed`.
2. **Slice for build.** `navigator:planner` cuts the work into batches. Tier 1 is everything that turns the 22 RED tests green plus the structural core (envelope and state types, evidence-carrying observation, the provider port, the workflow fixes). Tier 2 is deferred as recorded follow-ups, per the CLAUDE.md deferral rule:
   - the data-driven target catalog
   - the module split
   - the fault-injection simulator's larger variants
   - the workspace-hack crate
3. **No more gate loops.** Each batch is accepted by executable checks (named RED tests green, contract tests) and my cargo gate.

**Two things I need from you:**
1. **Tag template.** Did you intend to rename the CLI tag from `callisto-cli@{version}` to `callisto@{version}`? If not, I revert it in one line and drop the `previous-tag-templates` machinery, and the installer issue disappears. If yes, that migration lands in Tier 2.
2. **Scope cut.** Is Tier 1 for this PR right, with Tier 2 as tracked follow-ups? I recommend it. A full build of all 80 criteria is likely many hours of agent time at current cargo speeds. I'll refine the estimate after planning.

**Engineering defaults I'd apply unless you object:**
- Registry observation over the profile-bound HTTP endpoint, with a neutral-cwd `cargo info --registry crates-io` as a fallback batch if HTTP slips.
- Draft, upload, then publish for GitHub Releases, with `--prerelease`.
- Crates-only recovery for a source without `[release]`.
- A targeted `recovery-checks` job instead of the full `verify`.
- Manifest schema bump and rename of `source_commit` to `coordinator_commit`.
- Plain `http` allowed only for loopback registry endpoints.
- `[release]` treated as Callisto-self for now, with one constants table that derives the workflow matrices.

Yes, we had talked about making product tags. Cargo should not be running slow, you need to figure out why. It should take minutes, not hours. WTF. Don't overrun, don't run too much in parallel because of contention. Figure the fuck out vs assuming that is normal.

---
name: cargo-slowness-target-pollution
description: Diagnosed root cause of hours-long cargo builds/tests in callisto (2026-09-18): polluted target/debug (1.7M .o files); fix, prevention, and the one-invocation-shape rule.
metadata:
  type: project
---

Cargo builds/tests took 9-60 min per run for weeks because `target/debug/deps` had accumulated **1.72M `.o` files (180 GB apparent)** since 2026-07-25. macOS dev profile defaults to `split-debuginfo=unpacked`, which keeps every codegen unit's `.o`; stale hashes are never garbage-collected. The same workspace built cold in a fresh target dir in **31 s** and ran 7 test binaries in **12 s** (vs ~7 min stalls before). Machine, disk, AV, Spotlight were ruled out by measurement (fs create 18k/s, stat 470k/s, same inside and outside the project).

**Why:** the user was rightly angry that "cargo should take minutes, not hours"; I had wrongly treated the slowness as normal for several hours and let agents pile builds on it.

**How to apply:**
- Before blaming the machine: `ls target/debug/deps | wc -l`. Healthy is roughly 10k. If above ~100k, `mv target/debug target/debug.stale` and delete it in the background, then rebuild (31 s).
- Set `CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_SPLIT_DEBUGINFO=off` on agent/CI-local cargo runs: measured 0 `.o` files, 1,074 vs 7,924 files, no build-time cost. (`debug=line-tables-only` does NOT help.) It removes line-number debug info on macOS; a repo-level `[profile.dev]` change is the owner's call.
- Use ONE cargo invocation shape (`-p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph -p callisto-model` with `--test` names, or `--workspace`): different `-p` selections unify features differently (serde_core, rustix, getrandom, regex-syntax differ), forcing gix-* rebuilds and creating new stale hashes.
- One cargo owner at a time; do not let parallel agents build. Agents must never `pkill`/`kill` processes they did not start (a baseline agent ran `pkill -9 rustc` machine-wide).
- Related: [[feedback-diagnose-dont-guess-environment-issues]].

content.text:
**Cargo is fixed.** The workspace tests now run in about 2 minutes. That is the cold build of the three crates plus 991 passing tests and 22 parked ones (0 failures), where graph alone used to take 17 minutes. It was measured while the old `target/debug` was still deleting in the background.

**Cause:** `target/debug/deps` had piled up 1.72 million `.o` files (180 GB apparent size) since July 25. macOS dev builds keep every codegen unit's object file by default, and stale ones are never garbage-collected. I had wrongly treated the slowness as normal, and I was wrong about that. What I ruled out by measurement:
- **Machine:** an M3 Pro on AC power with no throttling and load under 3.
- **Disk:** file-system speed is the same inside and outside the project.
- **Security or indexing agents:** none found.

**What I measured:**

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Cold build, 3 crates | 9m16s | 31s |
| 7 test binaries | ~7 min of stalls | 12s |
| Files in `deps/` | 1.74M | 1,074 |

**What I changed:**
- I moved the old `target/debug` aside and am deleting it niced in the background.
- I added a local `.cargo/config.toml` with `split-debuginfo = "off"`, excluded via `.git/info/exclude` so it isn't committed. In my measurement it produced zero `.o` files. It drops line-number debug info from macOS dev binaries. A repo-level setting would be your call.
- I saved the diagnosis and rules to memory: one invocation shape, no parallel builds, no process killing.

**Not done, so you know the state:**
- The three W1 specs are unaccepted and untracked in `.claude/specs/`. They are also larger than what we need, and I won't use them for gating.

1. EVIDENCE-CARRYING OBSERVATION. Replace the bare ProviderObservationV1 { Absent, Exact, Conflict, Indeterminate } with Absent | Exact { evidence } | Conflict { reason } | Indeterminate { cause }. Evidence is a closed, per-role typed enum built from what providers can PROVE today: registry version (checksum and yanked as Option, filled where the provider can, None where it cannot yet), git tag (peeled commit), forge release (tag name, draft flag), artifact upload (size, sha256). Conflict reasons and indeterminate causes are closed enums derived from the cases the current provider code already distinguishes (tag points elsewhere, unannotated tag, forge release differs, asset differs, registry version exists but unobserved, provider status, command failure, malformed output, unsupported provider such as PyPI, timeout). An Exact evidence whose variant does not match the operation's role must be unrepresentable or rejected at the single constructor the receipt uses. The receipt's per-operation observations must carry the evidence (non-vacuous). Update the receipt wire schema version and the JSON schema snapshot/guard tests (see crates/callisto-cli/tests/schema_guard_test.rs and wherever schemars output is checked in) coherently. Provide two token types produced ONLY from an observation: AbsentProof (from Absent) and ExactEvidence (from Exact); later steps require them.

**Plan for what you asked not to defer.** The batches run one at a time, and each gets my independent gate:
- **S1, running:** evidence-carrying observations, the run envelope persisted before any effect, and one state-transition table with the "Attempting needs an Absent proof" guard.
- **S2a:** the `ReleaseProvider` port and the split of the 2,900-line `release.rs`, as a pure refactor.
- **S2b:** registry observation through the crates.io sparse index (yanked and checksum evidence), PyPI observation through its JSON API, and bounded retry honouring `Retry-After`.
- **S3:** the contract tier (fixtures captured from the real tools, strict fakes, and real-tool flag checks) and a fault-injection simulator that crashes at every persistence point.
- **S4:** a drift test so the four-target table can't diverge across the workflow, script, installer and `callisto.toml`.
- **Final:** independent adversarial review, and a real GitHub dry-run of the workflow with your go-ahead, since that means pushing the branch.

Two items I'm still leaving out deliberately, and why:
- **Data-driven `[release]` catalog for other adopters.** Only Callisto uses it today, and the drift test removes the duplication risk.
- **`workspace-hack` crate.** The pollution fix removed the pain.

Say if you want either one anyway.
Why have ci and ci fast?

They differ only in coverage. `ci` runs fmt-check, lint, test, audit, doc-check, wasm-check and `coverage`. `ci-fast` is the same without `coverage`. The justfile comment says why the split exists:
- **CI parity.** Real CI already runs coverage as its own parallel job on a separate runner.
- **Cost.** Locally, coverage is a full-workspace recompile under `llvm-cov` instrumentation, tacked onto the end of a serial pipeline.
- **Purpose.** Coverage numbers are a reporting concern, not something every local run needs.

That reason is really a workaround for slow builds. The split was probably added when local cargo was already crawling, and the polluted `target/` I just cleaned up made every one of those recompiles worse. I haven't timed `just coverage` on the clean tree. `ci-fast` takes about 4 minutes.

If instrumented coverage now takes a few minutes, I'd collapse them into a single `ci`. Two names for nearly the same check invite people to run the weaker one and think they matched CI. I can time it after S1 finishes, since S1 holds the cargo lock, and then propose the change. Do you want that?
For our workflow in GH actions can we just switch to ci being fast + coverage

- **GitHub workflow:** unchanged. It never called either recipe. It already runs each check, coverage included, as separate parallel jobs, and those job names are your required merge checks. Collapsing them into one job would rename the checks and require a ruleset update, so I'd leave them.
- **Docs:** `CLAUDE.md` and `ARCHITECTURE.md` updated to match.
- **S1:** still running.
